guarantees.claim: cmd_consty_err_d is asserted when cmd_chk is high and enables_q differs from enables_d; otherwise it retains the previous error state via cmd_consty_err_q.
one_hot_err_d is asserted when any bit of (enables_d & enables_sub) is high; otherwise it retains the previous error state via one_hot_err_q.

assumptions.claim: enables_q must be a previously sampled version of enables_d when cmd_chk is asserted, so that the comparison reflects command stability.
assumptions.risk: If enables_q is not the correct snapshot, cmd_consty_err_d may not flag a genuine command inconsistency, allowing corrupted commands.

formal_sketch.consequent: enables_q must be a previously sampled version of enables_d when cmd_chk is asserted, so that the comparison reflects command stability

assumptions.claim: enables_sub is defined such that (enables_d & enables_sub) != 0 indicates a one-hot violation (multiple enables active).
assumptions.risk: If enables_sub is incorrectly defined, one_hot_err_d may miss actual one-hot violations or trigger false positives.

formal_sketch.consequent: enables_sub is defined such that (enables_d & enables_sub) != 0 indicates a one-hot violation (multiple enables active)

security_implications: This chunk implements sticky error detection for command consistency (enables mismatch) and one-hot violation. These errors are part of a security countermeasure (SEC_CM) to ensure key manager commands are not corrupted and only one sub-command is active. If these error flags are not properly captured, cleared, or acted upon, the key manager could operate on tampered commands, potentially leading to incorrect key derivation, key extraction, or leakage of secret material.
